questions.q: Why are trace flags 1117 and 1118 described as "functionally retired" in this lesson?
options: Since SQL Server 2016, their behavior (equal filegroup autogrow and uniform full-extent allocation) is simply the default for every database, so the flags have nothing left to turn on
They were removed entirely from SQL Server and now cause a syntax error
They only ever worked on SQL Server 2005 and earlier
They were replaced by a single sp_configure option called 'legacy trace flags'
questions.explain: TF 1117 and TF 1118's effects became default database behavior starting with SQL Server 2016, making the flags redundant on modern versions.

questions.q: What is the modern, per-database equivalent of trace flag 4199's effect?
options: ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET QUERY_OPTIMIZER_HOTFIXES = ON, applied without a server restart
Restarting the SQL Server service with the -T4199 startup parameter is the only way to enable it
sp_configure 'optimizer hotfixes', 1 followed by RECONFIGURE
There is no per-database equivalent; TF 4199 can only be set instance-wide
questions.explain: Since SQL Server 2016, QUERY_OPTIMIZER_HOTFIXES as a database-scoped configuration setting gives the same effect as TF 4199, per database, without a restart.

questions.q: What is Lock Pages in Memory (LPIM), and how is it configured?
options: A Windows local security policy privilege (SeLockMemoryPrivilege) granted to the SQL Server service account, preventing the OS from trimming SQL Server's memory under pressure — not an sp_configure option
An sp_configure option set via EXEC sp_configure 'lock pages in memory', 1
A database-scoped configuration setting applied per database
A trace flag enabled at SQL Server startup with -T
questions.explain: LPIM is granted through Windows local security policy (secpol.msc) to the service account, and requires a SQL Server service restart to take effect.

questions.q: What does Instant File Initialization (IFI) actually skip, and what does it NOT apply to?
options: It skips zero-filling newly allocated space in data files on creation, restore, or autogrow; it never applies to the transaction log, which is always zero-initialized for crash recovery
It skips writing transaction log records entirely, for both data and log files
It skips running CHECKDB after a restore
It applies equally to both data files and log files, skipping zero-fill for both
questions.explain: IFI applies only to data files; the transaction log must always be zero-initialized because crash recovery depends on it.

questions.q: A colleague suggests enabling trace flags 1117 and 1118 on a brand-new SQL Server 2022 instance because an older tuning guide recommends it. Per this lesson, what should you check first?
options: Whether the version already provides that behavior by default (it does, since 2016) or offers the same control at the database level instead, rather than blindly applying an old recommendation
Whether the instance has Lock Pages in Memory enabled, since that is a prerequisite for those trace flags
Whether the classifier function has been configured for Resource Governor
Nothing; the trace flags should be applied exactly as the guide describes on every version
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that several once-essential trace flags are now default behavior or available as database-scoped settings, so applying them unchecked on a modern version is outdated advice.
